question: Parcels with a value of less than EUR 150 sent from non-EU countries are not subject to a customs duty but should theoretically incur an import turnover tax and (depending on the type of product) a sales tax. In practice, however, these two taxes are paid only in exceptional circumstances. First of all, non-EU traders like Temu only enclose a delivery note.

Invoices showing the applicable taxes are hard to come by in practice, even upon repeated request. What is more, given the sheer volume of packages and parcels (approximately 900 000 per day), it is virtually impossible to levy charges. No import service has the capacity for this. 1.
According to the Commission’s estimates, what is the economic damage to each individual Member State as a result of the above?
What action is the Commission considering to remedy this discrepancy?
answer: Since the entry into force of new value added tax (VAT) rules for e-commerce on 1 July 2021, VAT is due for all commercial imports regardless their value. In all cases an electronic customs declaration must be lodged, also for consignments of a value up to EUR 150 exempted from customs duties.

The most used method for collecting the VAT on low-value consignments (with a value up to EUR 150) is the Import One Stop Shop (IOSS), where VAT is paid upfront at the time of the sale. This system is currently used in more than 90% of the e-commerce shipments. In the first 18 months after the entry into force of the new VAT legislation, it has allowed Member States to collect an additional EUR 3.5 billion of VAT.

The VAT in the digital age (ViDA) legislative initiative, proposed on 8 December 2022 (1) and already supported by the Parliament, is currently negotiated in the Council. It would further strengthen the import one stop shop by requiring e-commerce operators to register and would allow customs to use this information for risk analysis. This will improve VAT collection efficiency and reduce VAT fraud.

Furthermore, Member States’ VAT legislation can determine that the Union Customs Code (UCC) is applicable on the import VAT. On 17 May 2023, the Commission put forward new proposals to reform the EU Customs Union, including the abolition of the current duty exemption for goods with a value up to EUR 150.

The Commission proposes that the e-commerce platforms charge duties (including VAT) on products sold online, at the time of sale, and make this information available to customs. While the negotiations in the Council are ongoing, on 13 March 2023 the Parliament adopted its position on the customs reform, largely supporting the ideas proposed by the Commission.
